body.text: The United States is undergoing a far-reaching transformation that holds implications for US partners in every corner of the globe. Countries, especially those in Southeast Asia, that have benefited from the principles the US has traditionally embodied and advanced, need to understand the changes underway to craft policies that reflect the country the US is becoming rather than the country it has historically been.

Despite liberal and conservative presidencies, economic booms and busts, jarring social fractures, and a dramatically evolving global economic and geopolitical landscape, the defining national character of the US has remained essentially the same throughout the post-WWII era.

The US had been a country that seeks to engage and lead constructively on the global stage. It has been the driving force behind rules-based multilateral institutions, free markets, and reduced trade barriers. Through developmental assistance and funding provided to civic organisations, media, and political parties, it had been a staunch advocate for democratic principles and the rule of law. The quality and integrity of its democratic institutions had often set the global standard. It had — rhetorically, if not always in practice — stood firmly against authoritarianism and crony capitalism.
Despite glaring examples of hypocrisy and the pursuit of its self-interest throughout its history, the US had, by and large, reflected these principles.

These definitional foundations of the post-war US national identity are now eroding. While President Trump has been the catalyst for many of these changes, he has, in other instances, simply intensified trendlines that had already been brewing for years.
Three aspects of the US transformation are especially noteworthy:

• The rise of an “imperial presidency”. The historical diffusion of power across US governance structures — created by the Constitutional system of checks and balances — is giving way to the concentrated power of an “imperial presidency”.

• A fraying democracy and declining institutional integrity. Democratic institutions, principles, and norms, particularly those involving the electoral process and the level of confidence in election results, have been weakened. The overall quality of democracy in the US is degrading.

• Declining faith in “globalism”. The longstanding US belief that cooperative global institutions and agreements, reduced trade barriers, and deepening economic integration best serve US national interests is being replaced by a growing sense that what is broadly referred to as “globalism” has disadvantaged the US. There is a deep sense across the political spectrum that the US should no longer play its traditional role on the global stage. Respect for mutually agreed multilateral rules — which in many instances the US championed — is now seen as hamstringing US ability to protect its national interests.

What happens in the US does not stay in the US. Its unique historical role, along with its economic, technological, and military might, means that US partners in Southeast Asia and beyond will be greatly impacted by the transformation now underway. Regional leaders need to consider three fundamental questions:
• In what ways is the US transforming, and what are the factors driving this shift?
• How will the US transformation manifest on the global stage and in its economic and strategic relationships with other countries?
• How should the nations of Southeast Asia reorient policies and approaches to reflect the new realities?
UNDERSTANDING THE TRANSFORMATION
Few changes underway in the US will be more impactful than the breakdown in the system of governmental checks and balances and the resulting emergence of an empowered “imperial presidency”.

The issue of presidential power was hotly debated by the authors of the US Constitution. Having just fought a bloody revolution to throw off the yoke of a mercurial and all-powerful king in England, the US founding fathers were determined to ensure that the powers of the US president were sufficient but not excessive.

The executive and legislative branches were intended to jointly conduct the operations of government, while the third branch — the judiciary — was envisioned as an impartial arbiter, ensuring that the other two branches operate in accordance with US law and the US Constitution.
Although imperfect, government policy developed in this manner throughout US history. It is no longer, however, an accurate description of the governance and policy process in the US.

Today, US policy increasingly flows from the individual whims of the president and his personal predilections rather than as the result of a deliberative process engaged in by co-equal branches of government.

Examples abound, especially when it comes to trade policy. Although it would have seemed astonishing in previous presidencies, it barely raised eyebrows when President Trump decided to increase the reciprocal tariff assessed on Switzerland from 30% to 39% simply because of personal antipathy he felt for that country’s leader during a phone conversation.

Trade policy will continue to remain more centralised in the executive branch. For US trade partners, this means a less technocratic and less predictable trade policy. The US commitment to ensuring a cooperative rules-based global order will continue to ebb.
There has never been a previous era during which US trade policy has been driven by highly subjective non-trade considerations such as these.

The rise of an imperial presidency has been aided and abetted by a compliant legislative branch. Particularly in the area of trade, Congress — which has been mandated by the Constitution to regulate “commerce with foreign nations” — has, over the decades, voluntarily ceded authority for conducting trade policy to the executive branch.

Congress, which was initially conceived as a coequal counterweight to the President, now functions almost as a subsidiary branch of the executive. Trump’s ability to bring Congress to heel has certainly been aided by the fact that the Republicans maintain majorities in both houses of Congress. While control of both houses is contested in elections every two years (held next in November 2026), even in a potential future scenario in which different parties control the executive and legislative branches, the gradual institutional transfer of power from the legislature to the executive will not be reversed anytime soon.

The rise of an imperial presidency has also been hastened by a series of favourable Supreme Court rulings handed down by a court now dominated by Trump-appointed conservatives. The Supreme Court has, nonetheless, also shown a willingness to rule against the administration, perhaps most prominently when it struck down the administration’s use of the International Economic Emergency Powers Act (IEEPA) to implement reciprocal tariffs. The administration accepted the decision and pivoted away from IEEPA as it seeks to reconstitute the reciprocal tariff regime under different legal instruments.

In other cases, however, particularly involving lower court decisions related to the administration’s immigration policies, the administration has not always fully or expeditiously comported with adverse rulings. While the Constitutional authority of the judicial branch has by and large been respected, the lackadaisical implementation of lower court rulings chips away at the judiciary’s ability to serve as a check on the executive branch.
DEGRADATION OF US DEMOCRATIC NORMS AND INSTITUTIONS

While there is no question that the US remains a functioning democracy, legitimate questions can be raised over the health of its democracy. Entrenched and intensified political polarisation — which has deepened in recent years and appears to be further calcifying — along with claims of election fraud levelled by the President himself, has degraded confidence in what Abraham Lincoln famously referred to as government “of the people, for the people, and by the people”.
The process of electing a US president has also evolved in ways not entirely consistent with a truly representative form of government.

Long before Presidential voting takes place, the electoral votes of the vast majority of states are already a foregone conclusion. A handful of “swing states” — states that could go either Democratic or Republican — essentially determine the presidency.

In a country of 330 million citizens (in which over 156 million votes were cast in the last presidential election), it has become increasingly common over recent electoral cycles for a tiny pool of 50,000 or 60,000 voters spread out across several swing states to effectively determine the presidency.

While presidential candidates nominally conduct “national” campaigns, the focus of their campaigns and the policies they advocate are, unsurprisingly, geared towards appealing to a small number of swing voters in a small number of swing states.

This is problematic for the trade-dependent economies of Southeast Asia. Although the exact list of “swing states” can vary slightly from election to election, it is almost always dominated by “rust belt” states — i.e., states that have seen their manufacturing base decimated by import competition under free trade policies pursued in recent decades.

Candidates attempting to win over voters in “rust belt” states such as Michigan, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin typically vie to out-duel each other in advocating higher tariffs and increased trade barriers. There is no significant constituency in these states supporting free trade.
IMPLICATIONS FOR SOUTHEAST ASIA

Understanding the far-reaching transformations underway in the US, Southeast Asian leaders need to reset perceptions of the US and retrench policies and approaches to mitigate risks while still engaging constructively where possible. As they navigate this tricky terrain, regional leaders should bear the following in mind:

Anti-globalisation in the US intensifies trade/national security linkages. The domestic backlash against globalism in the US is dovetailing with external concerns. As the US faces its most significant geopolitical rival — China — since the collapse of the Soviet Union, economic relationships are shaped, and frequently subordinated to, national security.

Perceptions, correct or incorrect, that China is responsible for hollowing out the US manufacturing base, have amplified the view of China as a “threat”. This view of China as a “threat” holds implications for Southeast Asian exporters, who could face higher US tariffs on products containing Chinese inputs deemed a “national security threat” under the US’s ever-widening definition of the term.

Conceptually, the premise that national security considerations can permit countries to abrogate rules and impose restrictions has been in existence at least since the establishment of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade in 1947. National security exceptions have been included in trade and other agreements since then. Recognising that the use of these provisions, however, could be readily abused and potentially unravel broader relationships among countries, they have been sparingly invoked.

Under the Trump administration, the definition of “national security” has been expanded beyond recognition to justify virtually anything the President wants to do in trade and economic relations. It has been used (or threatened) as a justification for raising tariffs, imposing export controls, or blocking investments.

The amorphous nature of “national security” and the difficulty in establishing precise definitional criteria is ideally suited to the consolidation of power within the executive branch, and adds fuel to the rise of an imperial presidency. Trump has been more willing than any predecessor to avail himself of this power, sometimes producing head-scratching conclusions. For instance, automotive tariffs on Japan have been threatened based on the supposition that a Honda Accord parked in an American garage constituted a national security threat.

An imperial US presidency with concentrated powers and a wide degree of discretion in defining threats to US national interests will be problematic for Southeast Asia. Countries will need not only to manage their bilateral relationships with the US, but also to be skilful in navigating an increasingly complicated US-China-Southeast Asia triangle. Given the deep economic integration between Southeast Asia and China, regional leaders need to anticipate an intensifying scrutiny from the US and a willingness on its part to invoke a remarkably broad definition of national security as a justification for punitive trade actions aimed at reducing the region’s economic interaction with China.

Regional leaders will need to make judgment calls in specific cases as to whether their own national interests are best served by complying with US pressure; the starting point for strategising should, however, be a recognition that for the US, national security considerations — particularly in the context of the US-China rivalry — trump all.

Collapsing US-brokered stability raising costs and uncertainties. Even the harshest critics of US conduct during the post-war era would acknowledge that the US has also delivered a range of global “public goods” that have supported stability and economic development. This has been especially true for Southeast Asia, where many countries have capitalised on a generally benign global environment, declining trade barriers, and expanding exports to climb the economic development ladder.

With over 80% of global trade being conducted by sea, the US’s traditional role of guarantor of open international shipping lanes has provided an incalculable “public good”. The war in Iran and the closure of the Straits of Hormuz have painfully illustrated the extent to which Southeast Asia (and others) depend on open sea lanes for their economic well-being. This also further reflects the implications of an imperial presidency on Southeast Asia. Trump launched the US into this war without Congressional consultation or approval, based on dubious grounds, and Southeast Asia is presented with a bill for significantly higher energy prices as a result.

The US’ interest in and capacity to continue playing its traditional role on the global stage are on the decline, reflecting the growing antipathy towards “globalism” and the sense frequently articulated by Trump that others need to “pay” for US “services” through tariffs or shoulder the burden themselves.

Regional leaders now need to adjust policies and approaches to reflect a new world in which open sea lanes and a mostly benign global environment can no longer be considered a given. Rising costs are likely to ripple across economies. Insurance rates for the shipping lines that make trade possible are increasing to reflect declining stability and businesses are in some cases eschewing the most economically efficient products and services in favour of more secure but higher cost options.
There has been an immensely beneficial “US-brokered stability dividend” throughout the post-war era. Expect that dividend to decline.

Back to the Gilded Age? Trump has intertwined public policy and business interests (including his own) to an extent not seen since the Gilded Age — an era characterised by flourishing crony capitalism.

Tariff rates are raised dramatically, but companies can apply for exceptions that are granted or denied based on opaque criteria. (Southeast Asian countries benefited from this process as exemptions were granted on, for example, consumer electronic products they produce, as a result of lobbying by tech giants such as Dell, HP, and Apple). Trade deals oblige foreign countries to invest billions in the US, with the President alone determining which companies reap the windfall. Family members are negotiating business deals in foreign countries that have significant policy issues pending before the US government. Against this backdrop, Trump has embarked on an ambitious fundraising campaign to pay for a series of vanity projects, including a triumphal arch that has been dubbed the “Arch de Trump” and a massive White House ballroom for entertaining.

Critics have been quick to seize upon public disclosures indicating that Trump’s personal wealth increased by US$2.2 billion in 2025, but it is important to note that there is no evidence of wrong-doing on the part of the president or his family members, and no suggestion of wrong-doing should be implied or inferred. At the same time, leaders should understand that an environment has been created in the US that has historically proved conducive to crony capitalism.
LASTING IMPACT?

In some respects, Trump is likely to remain sui generis in the annals of the US Presidency. We are unlikely to see, for example, a continuation of the rather bizarre personalisation of trade policy that Trump has pursued, adjusting tariff rates based on either the antipathy or respect he has for a given country’s leader. The maddening policy shifts, in which trade actions are taken and then reversed on a moment’s notice, are also unlikely to be a feature of future presidencies.

In other respects, however, the Trump transformation is likely to endure. Once the toothpaste is squeezed out of the tube, it cannot easily be put back in. Future presidents will not be inclined to curtail the expanded powers Trump has bequeathed them. Trade policy will continue to remain more centralised in the executive branch. For US trade partners, this means a less technocratic and less predictable trade policy. The US commitment to ensuring a cooperative rules-based global order will continue to ebb.

There is no national leader on the horizon in either party that is advocating for a return to the country’s traditional pro-free trade policies. The political spectrum in the US has shifted for the foreseeable future. But irrespective of what may follow Trump, there are still 2.5 years of the Trump Presidency for regional leaders to navigate.
RECOMMENDATIONS
How should the region respond? The most relevant recommendations apply equally from Bangkok to Jakarta and all points in between:

• Deepen efforts at diversification: the changes underway in the US mean it has become a considerably less reliable partner than at any other time in the post-war era. While the US cannot be entirely “replaced”, an expanded web of trade and investment relationships will provide some degree of insulation from US vicissitudes.

• Pursue high-quality trade agreements: US belligerence has had a corrosive effect on the trade rules the region has relied on for prosperity. Existing WTO rules are woefully inadequate, and updates are unlikely. For the trade-dependent economies of the region, the pursuit (or revision) of deep-integration trade agreements that strengthen resilience and rules will be essential.

• Calibrate China relationship: the US high-tariff regime means that China’s subsidised excess industrial capacity will continue to be exported into the region, oftentimes with devastating impact on domestic producers. Trade frictions with China are undesirable, but significant domestic manufacturing dislocations are equally unpalatable. A closing US market means that countries in the region must be prepared — when necessary — to apply trade remedy laws against China.
